cards.explanation: The answer is Solomon's carriage. Verse 7 says so right away: “Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage, escorted by sixty of the mightiest men of Israel.” The one coming up from the wilderness is described “…like a column of smoke, scented with myrrh and frankincense…” (Song of Solomon 3:6). Solomon is Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1). Smoke and spices, friends. That's an entrance.

The answer is False. It's sixty, not twelve. The poem says the carriage is escorted by “…sixty of the mightiest men of Israel.” That's a lot of swords walking beside one carriage. I'd feel very safe, and very watched.

The answer is the terror of the night. The text says each man has his sword at his side, “…prepared for the terror of the night.” These men are skilled with the sword and experienced in warfare. So when the lights go out, they're ready. I wouldn't want to be whatever the night is sending.

The answer is love from the daughters of Jerusalem. The poem says the interior is “…inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.” The posts are silver, the base is gold and the seat is purple fabric, but the inside gets something better. Fancy wood is nice, friends. That's nicer.

The answer is the daughters of Zion. The poem says, “Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon…” They're invited to look at the king in his crown. The text says it's the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding. Big day, friends.

The answer is wedding. The verse says Solomon wears “…the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding…” His mother is the one placing it on his head. A king's mother crowning him on his wedding day is a proud moment.

The answer is False, because none are missing. The groom says her teeth are like newly shorn sheep coming up from the washing, and “each has its twin, and not one of them is lost.” It's a picture of a full, matched set. I'd call that a perfect count.

The answer is tower. The groom says her neck is like “…the tower of David, built with rows of stones…” A thousand shields of warriors hang on it. David is Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), and his tower is a strong, proud picture. He is saying something grand about her.

The answer is True. After picture after picture, the groom says, “You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw.” He doesn't pick out one part. He says all of her. That's a man with only good things to say.

The answer is a wild and dangerous place. Dens of lions and mountains of leopards don't sound like a vacation spot, friends. The groom says, “Come with me from Lebanon, my bride…” and calls her down from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards. I think he wants her out of that rough country and beside him. I'd take that invitation too.

The answer is True. The groom says, “you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your neck.” One glance. That's all it took. Me, I smell one fresh batch coming out of the oven and I'm done for.

The answer is False, because wine loses. The groom says, “How delightful is your love, my sister, my bride! Your love is much better than wine…” Her love comes out ahead of wine, and her perfume beats all spices. In this poem, her love wins.

The answer is False, because the garden is closed up. The groom says, “My sister, my bride, you are a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed.” A locked garden isn't open to just anyone. The poem says it three different ways.

The answer is Lebanon. The verse says, “You are a garden spring, a well of fresh water flowing down from Lebanon.” Lebanon has been in the poem before, in his call to come with him from there. Now fresh water pours down from it.

The answer is the north and south winds. The call is “Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind. Breathe on my garden and spread the fragrance of its spices.” Both winds are called to breathe on the garden. That garden is full of spices, and the winds are asked to spread the fragrance.

The answer is the beloved. The call says, “Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits.” The beloved is the one invited in. The garden was described as locked up in verse 12, so this invitation matters, friends. The beloved is the one asked to taste the choicest fruits.
The answer is True. The groom says, “I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride…” That comes in 5:1, right after the call in 4:16. The call went out, and he says he has come.

The answer is eat and drink. The line in 5:1 says, “Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved.” The friends are told to eat and drink, and the second part says to drink freely. When a verse says eat, I'm listening.
